newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official to push green issues on Asian tour.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official to push green issues on Asian tour.

text.p: A senior State Department official on Wednesday starts a two-week trip to China, South Korea and Japan for talks on environmental issues ranging from toxic chemicals to the illegal trade in bear and rhino parts.
The visit by Assistant Secretary of State Eileen Claussen comes at a time when the Clinton administration is seeking to combine green initiatives with foreign policy.

Claussen, who will be in the region from Oct. 18 to Nov. 4, is to meet officials from all three countries to discuss global climate concerns, production and trade of toxic chemicals, illegal wildlife trade, fisheries and forestry issues, a department official said. She will spend most of her time in China, a growing source of environmentalists' concern.
"By 2010 China will surpass the United States as the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases," Marcia Aronoff of the Environmental Defence Fund said.

"China is extraordinarily important in addressing a whole range of critical environmental issues starting with global warming, the oceans and wildlife," Jacob Scherr of the Washington-based Natural Resources Defence Council said.
"Decisions to be made in China regarding transportation, automobiles, refrigerators are going to be very, very important," he addded.

Ongoing international talks on how to curb heat-trapping pollution after 2000 are set to culminate at the end of 1997 in Japan but are not expected to include new controls on industry or cars in developing countries.

But manufacturing and fossil energy groups in Western nations insist that rapidly developing countries like China and India should not be allowed to use cheap, dirty fuel if industrialised countries are forced to trim their emissions.

Another key issue in the U.S. talks with China and South Korea will be the multi-billion dollar trade in endangered wildlife, including rhino, tiger and bear parts, which are highly valued in traditional medicine.
U.S. officials do not expect to reach specific agreements on the East Asia trip.
